title: Chinese marks: imperial reign marks (Ming, Qing, Hongxian) and hall and studio marks
applies_to: Chinese imperial reign marks (nianhao) on porcelain and other works of art. A reading of the mark's characters (or its pinyin/Wade-Giles name) is matched to a reign. The decode names the reign the mark claims; it never dates the item, because marks of earlier reigns were copied for centuries.

caveats.text: A reign mark names the era it claims, not the date the object was made. Copied (apocryphal) marks of earlier reigns are extremely common, so a mark alone never dates a piece; judge body, glaze, shape, decoration and the quality of the writing first.

Copies were not always meant to deceive: Chinese potters put marks of admired earlier reigns on later wares out of reverence (in Chinese usage 寄托款 'homage mark' or 仿款 'imitation mark'). Auction catalogues call these 'apocryphal' marks.
Even marks of the reign itself are not proof of imperial manufacture: private kilns (民窑 minyao) also wrote the current reign's mark, usually less carefully than on official wares (官窑 guanyao).
Japanese potters also copied Chinese Ming marks, especially Jiajing and Wanli, on their own wares.

Era-year ranges follow the Western-calendar convention most reference tables use. A new era name normally took effect on the lunar New Year after the previous emperor's death, so the last Chinese year of an era usually ends in January or February of the following Western year; that is the source of most one-year differences between tables.

An empty double ring, or a symbol (leaf, lingzhi fungus, ruyi head) where a mark would be, is associated with the Kangxi reign after the local magistrate Zhang Qizhong forbade writing the reign name on porcelain in 1677 (the 16th year of Kangxi; the Jingdezhen taolu, bk. 8, quoting the county gazetteer). Some modern sources give 1667 and call it an imperial order; the Chinese record says 1677 and a magistrate. Empty rings occur in other periods too, so they do not date a piece.
Seal-script reign marks before the 18th century are rare, with one well-known exception: the four-character seal marks of Yongle (永樂年製).

The era name 祺祥 (Qixiang) was proclaimed for the boy emperor in 1861 and abolished within weeks, after the Xinyou coup, and replaced by Tongzhi. It never appears on porcelain; a few trial coins exist.

caveats: A Hongxian (洪憲) mark is almost always later: the court porcelain made for Yuan Shikai in 1915–16 is marked 居仁堂製 (Jurentang) in red seal script, and 洪憲年製 pieces are mostly 1920s–30s private-kiln wares or modern copies (Baidu Baike 洪宪瓷, citing the Palace Museum Journal; Maigoo; the Met dates its Hongxian-marked vases 1930s–40s).

caveats.text: Marks of earlier reigns were already written at the imperial kiln itself: Zhengde wares carry Xuande marks, and Chenghua wares copied Xuande designs. (Baidu Baike also reports sherds marked 大明宣德年製 from Chenghua layers excavated in 1987; no excavation report confirming it was found.) In the Ming, marks of earlier reigns are most common on Tianqi wares; under Kangxi, Xuande, Chenghua and Jiajing marks are common; from Guangxu to the Republic, Kangxi marks are the most copied.

reading.text: Read in vertical columns, top to bottom, with the columns taken from right to left.
A six-character mark is usually written in two columns of three or three columns of two; occasionally in one line, vertical or horizontal (a horizontal line reads right to left).
Six-character structure: characters 1-2 the dynasty (大明 Da Ming 'Great Ming' or 大清 Da Qing 'Great Qing'), 3-4 the era name, 5-6 年製 nian zhi 'made in the period'.
A four-character mark omits the dynasty and starts with the era name (e.g. 康熙年製).

Marks come in regular script (楷書 kaishu) or seal script (篆書 zhuanshu); seal marks are commonly arranged as a square block, typically three columns of two characters for six characters, sometimes inside a square border.

Seal-script reign marks before the 18th century are rare and should be viewed with suspicion; the well-known exception is the four-character Yongle mark 永樂年製. Seal marks became common from the Yongzheng reign on.
Variants: 御製 yu zhi 'made by imperial order' in place of 年製 (recorded for Kangxi, Yongzheng, Qianlong, Jiaqing); 造 zao 'made' occasionally in place of 製.

The mark is usually on the base, often in underglaze blue inside a double ring; also in iron-red, other enamels or gold over the glaze, incised, or impressed, and sometimes along the mouth rim or in a panel in the decoration.

republic_note.text: After the Qing abdication (12 February 1912) there is no imperial reign mark. Republic-period (1912-1949) porcelain often carries apocryphal Qing marks, especially Qianlong, on imitations of imperial enamelled wares (also 古月軒 Guyuexuan marks), or hall marks such as 居仁堂製 Jurentang, named for the hall where Yuan Shikai held his enthronement audience in December 1915 (Maigoo). A Jurentang mark therefore points to the Republic period, not to an imperial reign.

rows.imperial_marks_note: Official Hongwu porcelain is generally regarded as unmarked. Bushell (1899) knew only a few Hongwu-marked pieces 'of somewhat doubtful authenticity'; Hobson (1915) says few Hongwu-marked museum pieces even look Ming. A modern Shanghai Museum text quotes that Hongwu official wares carried no reign mark (洪武时不写年款).
rows.later_copies_note: Hongwu-marked pieces exist but are later; Hobson describes a British Museum dish with the mark that is about a century later than it claims.

rows.imperial_marks_note: Genuine Yongle marks are four characters, 永樂年製, in archaic seal script, and rare; most Yongle official wares are unmarked. They are incised or moulded under the glaze on sweet-white (甜白) cups and bowls, and painted in underglaze blue inside the famous press-hand cups (壓手杯), in the center of a lion-and-ball or flower medallion.
rows.later_copies_note: Hobson (1915) notes not-uncommon blue-and-white cups with a four-character Yongle mark that are 'hardly older than the last dynasty' (Qing).

marks.note: Standard imperial form: underglaze blue, two columns of three, usually in a double circle on the base; also written in one horizontal line below the mouth rim, and sometimes incised.
Rarer.
Seal forms on porcelain are regarded as later; the seal form is typical of bronze censers.

rows.imperial_marks_note: Imperial Xuande wares are commonly marked, in six-character regular script, typically in a double circle; Bushell also notes marks incised in the paste and the last four characters impressed as a seal. Marks are found in many places on the vessel (base, inside, neck, rim), some in one horizontal line; in the characters, 德 is written without the short stroke above 心.
rows.later_copies_note: One of the two most-copied Ming marks (with Chenghua). Already used apocryphally in the 16th century (Zhengde wares with 仿宣德款), very common on Kangxi-period porcelain, and on most 17th-18th-century bronze censers. Kangxi's imperial kiln also copied Xuande dishes.

rows.imperial_marks_note: Part of the mid-15th-century 'interregnum' or 'blank period' (空白期) of Zhengtong, Jingtai and Tianshun: official kiln wares of these reigns carry no reign marks. Records suggest reduced output rather than none, and excavations at the Jingdezhen imperial kiln site since 1988 have found official wares of the period, all unmarked.
rows.later_copies_note: None documented as a common copied mark. The Jingtai era name is well known on cloisonné enamel (景泰藍), not on porcelain.

marks.note: Standard imperial form in underglaze blue; within a double circle or, on small cups, a double square.
A single 天 in underglaze blue on the base of small doucai jars of the reign; copied under Qianlong.
Not established as a mark of the period: four-character Chenghua marks are generally later (one was used on Kangxi wares).

rows.imperial_marks_note: Imperial Chenghua wares carry the six-character regular-script mark. Genuine Chenghua porcelain is scarce. Regular script only, never seal; the double square frame first appears in this reign. Small doucai jars of the reign are marked with the single character 天 in underglaze blue (the 'tian jars'), a form later copied under Qianlong.
rows.later_copies_note: The most frequently copied mark of all (with Xuande). Used on 16th-century wares and, most of all, on Kangxi-period porcelain: Hobson says a fine Chenghua-marked piece can generally be assumed to be Kangxi; Gulland's editor notes the same. Also on many modern inferior wares.
rows.single_source_note: Personal name Zhu Jianshen from Wikipedia only (and its characters there look wrong). Double-square framing of Chenghua marks is seen in Gotheborg's mark notes only. Mark and copy notes now also in Baidu Baike; what stays single-sourced is the emperor's personal name or an older spelling.

Four syllables in the Phags-pa alphabet, the only Ming reign mark written in it: on Zhengde blue-and-white dragon wares (two in the Palace Museum) and on semi-finished bowls and dishes from the late-Zhengde layers excavated in 2014. The excavators read it as 正德年製; a press account glossed it as 至正年製, a Yuan reign name.

Wikipedia, Chinese Wikipedia, UCSD and Gulland give 1573-1620: the Wanli emperor died in the 7th month of 1620 and the era name ran until the Taichang era was applied retroactively from the 8th month of that year.

marks.note: Underglaze blue; Hobson illustrates an imperial vase with the mark on the neck.

rows.imperial_marks_note: Imperial Wanli wares commonly carry the six-character regular-script mark; more often seen than Longqing because the reign was long.
rows.later_copies_note: A favorite of Japanese copyists (with Jiajing), often on Imari wares.

rows.year_note: About four months of 1620 (8th to 12th month), applied retroactively by his successor; it shares the Western year 1620 with Wanli 48.
rows.imperial_marks_note: No Taichang marks recorded on porcelain ('apparently unrepresented', Hobson; 'conspicuous for their absence', Bushell).
rows.later_copies_note: None documented.

rows.year_note: 1621-1627 standard; Gulland and UCSD give 1620 as the start (accession year).

marks.note: Underglaze blue.

rows.imperial_marks_note: Tianqi-marked pieces are very rare and usually of inferior quality; official records are silent on the imperial kiln in the last Ming reigns.
rows.later_copies_note: None documented as common.

rows.year_note: Old porcelain books and UCSD end it in 1643; Wikipedia, Chinese Wikipedia and the NUS Ming Shi-lu table run it to April 1644, when the emperor died at the fall of Beijing.

marks.note: Underglaze blue.

rows.imperial_marks_note: Very rare; Hobson knew only a pair of wine cups in the British Museum. Bushell records a dedication dated Chongzhen 9th year (1636) on a temple vase.
rows.later_copies_note: None documented.

rows.year_note: 1644-1661 for China proper.

marks.note: Rare, on small enamelled and blue-and-white pieces in late-Ming style.
Considered fictitious; no genuine seal mark known.

rows.imperial_marks_note: Authentic Shunzhi-marked porcelain is very rare ('virtually unknown', Hobson).
rows.later_copies_note: Shunzhi seal marks are considered later inventions.

rows.year_note: Era officially from 1662; the emperor succeeded in 1661, so Gulland, UCSD-style accession tables and Hobson's footnote give 1661.

marks.note: Standard: underglaze blue, usually in a double ring, in two or three columns; marks became precise and small late in the reign.
Made by imperial order: the mark of the palace-workshop enamelled wares (falangcai), in blue or pink enamel within a double square.
Unframed four-character Kangxi marks point to the Guangxu period or later.
Disputed: Bushell had seen it on genuine pieces but notes it is often counterfeited; Gotheborg has not confirmed it on genuine Kangxi pieces. Very rare at best.

rows.imperial_marks_note: The Kangxi mark is relatively uncommon on early Kangxi porcelain: in 1677 (the 16th year of the reign) the district magistrate Zhang Qizhong (張齊仲) forbade the potters of Jingdezhen to write the emperor's reign name or the sages' words on porcelain, lest they be broken, and empty double rings or symbols took their place. Ming marks (Chenghua, Xuande, occasionally Jiajing) are common on Kangxi wares. Six-character regular-script marks become standard late in the reign. Enamelled palace wares (falangcai) carry 康熙御製 in a double square.
rows.later_copies_note: Freely used on 19th- and 20th-century wares; Hobson says the bulk of Kangxi-marked pieces are modern, and the Kangxi mark is almost invariable on late-19th-century blue-and-white imitations. Unframed four-character Kangxi marks point to the Guangxu period or later.

rows.year_note: 1723-1735; Gulland gives 1723-1736 (end = next start).

marks.note: Standard: underglaze blue, two columns of three in a double ring.
Occurs; Bushell says more rarely than regular script.
Including blue-enamel marks in a double square on enamelled palace wares.
'Made by imperial order' variant recorded by Bushell and Hobson.

rows.imperial_marks_note: Regular script dominates; seal-script reign marks begin to appear in this reign. Sources differ on emphasis: Christie's says seal marks 'found favour' in Yongzheng, Bushell says the seal form occurs more rarely.
rows.later_copies_note: Yongzheng marks appear on later imitations; Hobson thought most Yongzheng-marked pieces of his day were of the period and the imitations coarse. Yongzheng imperial wares themselves copied earlier wares with the earlier marks.

rows.year_note: 1736-1795; the emperor abdicated on the last day of the 60th year and lived to 1799.

marks.note: The usual form: three columns of two, mostly without a frame, in underglaze blue or iron-red; also gilt, incised or moulded.
Less common; Gotheborg ties it to the first years of the reign.
Used mostly early in the reign.
Including enamel marks.
'Made by imperial order' variant.

rows.imperial_marks_note: Seal script became the usual form for the imperial mark. Enamelled imperial wares often have the mark in red in a reserved panel on a turquoise-enamelled base (Hobson).
rows.later_copies_note: Heavily copied: on 19th-century and export wares, and especially Republic-period (1912-1949) imitations of Qing imperial enamelled wares; red-enamel seal marks are a favorite on later copies.

marks.note: Usual form.
Less frequent.
'Made by imperial order' variant (Bushell).

rows.imperial_marks_note: Seal script predominates, continuing Qianlong practice.
rows.later_copies_note: Hobson judged later reign marks rarely borrowed, so they generally indicate date; no common copying documented.
rows.single_source_note: Personal name from Wikipedia only; the later-copies judgment is Hobson's alone and is a 1915 opinion. Mark and copy notes now also in Baidu Baike; what stays single-sourced is the emperor's personal name or an older spelling.

marks.note: Usual form, often a square seal in underglaze blue or iron-red.
Less common.

rows.imperial_marks_note: Seal script predominates.
rows.later_copies_note: None documented as common.
rows.single_source_note: Personal name from Wikipedia only. Mark and copy notes now also in Baidu Baike; what stays single-sourced is the emperor's personal name or an older spelling.

rows.year_note: 1851-1861 standard. Bushell's Chinese Art gives 1851-60; Gulland 1851-1862.

marks.note: Bushell: imperial pieces usually marked in full, penciled in red in regular script.
Less common than regular script.

rows.imperial_marks_note: Marked Xianfeng pieces are scarce. The imperial kiln fired reduced orders in the first four years of the reign; from 1855 (the fifth year), with Jingdezhen in the war against the Taiping, palace porcelain stopped, and the kiln was not rebuilt until 1866. Wares fired in 1853 and 1854 waited at the kiln because the river route was cut. (Hobson and Baidu Baike put the kiln's destruction in 1853 and Bushell in the sixth year; the palace archives show firing continued into 1854.) From this reign on, regular script is again the usual imperial mark, replacing the seal script of Qianlong to Daoguang.
rows.later_copies_note: None documented.

rows.year_note: 1862-1874 standard (era ran into February 1875; emperor died January 1875). Gulland 1862-1875; Hobson vol. 2 has 1862-1873 in one heading (inconsistent with his own table).

marks.note: The usual imperial form: underglaze blue, two columns of three.
Incised or gilt, on teadust and flambé glazes.

rows.imperial_marks_note: The imperial kiln, idle from 1855, was rebuilt in 1866. Marked wares exist and are of modest quality by most accounts; regular script is usual, with seal script incised or gilt on teadust and flambé glazes. Wares made for the emperor's wedding (1872) carry the marks 燕喜同和 and 長春同慶 as well as the reign mark.
rows.later_copies_note: None documented.

rows.year_note: 1875-1908 (Wikipedia, UCSD, Gotheborg). Burton & Hobson and Hobson give 1875-1909, counting through the lunar year in which the emperor died (Xuantong era began January 1909).

marks.note: Usual imperial form (Bushell: 'usually marked in ordinary characters').
Four-character regular-script marks widely used in the period.
Also used, less often than regular script.

rows.imperial_marks_note: Regular script is usual on Guangxu imperial wares; related palace wares carry hall marks such as 大雅齋 and 儲秀宮製 (Empress Dowager Cixi).
rows.later_copies_note: The Guangxu period itself produced many copies with earlier marks, especially Kangxi on blue-and-white. Its own marks and the Cixi palace marks (大雅齋, 永慶長春, 體和殿製) were in turn copied in the Republic period.

rows.year_note: Era name in use from the lunar New Year of 1909; Puyi abdicated 12 February 1912. Hobson gives 1909-1911, Gotheborg 1909-1912, Burton & Hobson 1910-12, UCSD and Wikipedia (reign) 1908-1912.

marks.note: The usual imperial form: two columns, without a frame, mostly in underglaze blue.

rows.imperial_marks_note: Short reign with limited output; Hobson calls it 'a blank' in ceramic history. Marked imperial pieces exist but are uncommon.
rows.later_copies_note: None documented.

rows.year_note: Era name proclaimed 31 December 1915 for the year 1916, used from 1 January 1916 and abandoned 22 March 1916 (83 days). Gotheborg labels the period 1915-16.

marks.note: Most examples are later (see later_copies_note).
Variant named by the Chinese source; also largely later.

rows.imperial_marks_note: Porcelain actually made for Yuan's court (supervised at Jingdezhen by Guo Baochang 郭葆昌) is said to bear the hall mark 居仁堂製 (Jurentang) rather than a Hongxian reign mark; a 13-piece Jurentang set given by Yuan's daughter is in the Suzhou Museum.
rows.later_copies_note: Hongxian-marked porcelain is overwhelmingly later: dealers produced 洪憲年製 / 洪憲御製 marked wares after Yuan's death in 1916, and the Met dates its Hongxian-marked pair of vases to the 1930s-40s. Jurentang marks were also used on Republic-period wares.
rows.single_source_note: The claim that genuine Hongxian court porcelain bears Jurentang marks (and the Guo Baochang story) comes from one Chinese popular source; the Met's own wording about its mark was seen only in a search summary. Wade-Giles 'Hung-hsien' is from the Wikipedia infobox only. Mark and copy notes now also in Baidu Baike; what stays single-sourced is the emperor's personal name or an older spelling.

caveats.text: A hall mark names the hall, studio or palace building a piece was made for, or claims to be. Hall marks were copied too (慎德堂製 under Guangxu and in the Republic; 居仁堂製 after 1916), so the mark alone does not date the item or show that it is genuine.
Many hall names were used by more than one owner, and many private hall marks cannot be tied to a person: the same characters can belong to different households in different centuries.
